Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette: Sara, a 19-year-old North American woman, has been struggling intensely with symptoms following an assault she experienced several months ago. She is now married but unemployed, and her life has become significantly disrupted by the lingering effects of that traumatic event. The night of the assault was particularly brutal for Sara. As she walked home from a party where alcohol had been present, someone followed her through a dark alleyway. The sound of a motorcycle engine in the distance made her heart race as it seemed to get closer. Just before the attacker emerged, shouting voices in Arabic broke the silence, and the smell of alcohol on his breath triggered an immediate sense of dread. These auditory and olfactory cues have since become potent triggers for Sara. Since then, even the simplest sounds can set off a chain reaction within her. The roar of a motorcycle engine often sends her into a panic, causing her to retreat indoors and avoid going out at night altogether. She is also on edge when she hears Arabic being spoken in public places, associating it with that fateful encounter. Her husband has noticed how quickly Sara's demeanor changes in such situations; she becomes withdrawn, avoids social gatherings, and insists on staying home after dark. Sara's triggers do more than just cause immediate distress - they also lead to her using maladaptive strategies like avoiding anniversaries connected to the event, going out at night, or even paying attention to her own body. She is hyper-vigilant about anything that might remind her of the trauma and actively avoids situations where these cues could be present. Her memory of the assault remains vivid and intrusive. Something in her surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning. For instance, when she smells alcohol or hears shouting in Arabic, the memories flood back. She sometimes hears voices and smells odors that transport her right back to that night. This heightened recall makes it difficult for her to engage in daily activities, as even mundane events can trigger a flashback. The trauma has shattered Sara's beliefs about how the world works, leaving her feeling like she is no longer capable of doing what once defined her. She constantly questions why nobody else stopped the attack and wonders if she could have done more to prevent it herself. These negative appraisals fuel her sense of vulnerability and exacerbate her threat monitoring behaviors. She frequently listens for sounds that might indicate someone is entering her home, checks behind her to ensure no one is following, and feels like the assault could happen again at any moment. Sara's avoidance strategies have not only isolated her but also reinforced her negative beliefs about herself and others. Her husband has become concerned about how she now avoids social events and even simple tasks that might involve going out at night or being exposed to certain triggers. He notes that Sara seems to believe these precautions are necessary, further entrenching her sense of vulnerability. The combination of constant threat monitoring and intrusive memories creates a vicious cycle where each symptom reinforces the others. The more she avoids, the stronger her negative beliefs become, leading to heightened vigilance and an increased likelihood of being triggered by everyday events. This has left Sara feeling trapped in a world where she is constantly on guard, never fully able to relax or trust that such trauma won't repeat itself. What finally brought Sara to seek help was when she realized how these behaviors were affecting her relationship with her husband and her overall well-being. She feared becoming increasingly isolated and unable to cope with the simplest aspects of daily life. Despite the overwhelming sense of vulnerability, Sara is hopeful for a future where she can reclaim some normalcy without constantly living in fear. Sara's current state is one of profound anxiety and isolation, but she is determined to find ways to manage her symptoms and restore a sense of safety and control in her life.
